chapter_theme: Kurinjippattu entire: the friend discloses the secret love to the mother (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல்), telling how on the day the mother sent the girls to guard the millet they bathed, gathered the flowers of every land, were met by a hill hunter, were saved by him from a wild elephant, and how he embraced the girl, swore to marry her and has come every night since, through dangers the girl weeps over.
structure_note: One speech to the mother. Lines 1 to 34 give the reason for speaking; lines 35 to 106 the girls' day of play, with the list of flowers (62 to 96); lines 107 to 186 the man's arrival, the elephant and the union; lines 187 to 233 his land, his oath and his promise at sunset; lines 234 to 261 his nightly visits and the dangers of his path. Thirteen of the sixteen units were moved to sense breaks.

pattupattu:8:1-22.reading: The friend tells the mother that the girl's wasting sickness, which has loosened her bright ornaments and which the mother has tried to cure by asking diviners, praising, worshipping, strewing flowers and offering incense to gods of many forms, is a grief the girl hid until the friend forced her to speak; and since jewels of pearl, gem and gold can be mended when broken but lost worth and fame cannot be washed clean even by sages, she asks whether it is wrong to let the mother know that, passing their father's strict guard, the two chose this marriage themselves.
pattupattu:8:1-22.nuance: The friend's argument for speaking rests on irreparability: a broken ornament can be rejoined, but lost good name cannot be washed back even by the wisest, so silence now would cost what cannot be repaired. The mother's rites are not mocked, only shown to miss the cause. இருவேம் in line 21 most naturally means the lovers; it could also take in the friend, who calls the act hers too in line 32.

thinai_evidence.note: a love chosen in secret past the father's guard, to be disclosed: kalavu, kurinji's punarthal

comparisons.vehicle: முத்தினு மணியினும் பொன்னினு மத்துணை நேர்வருங் குரைய கலங்கெடிற் புணருஞ்
comparisons.tenor: worth, wonder and nature, which once lowered cannot be restored

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the text addresses அன்னாய் (line 1); whether the foster mother or the mother is meant is not said

pattupattu:8:23-34.reading: Saying that even if the union does not come by the proper path it will be theirs in the other world, the girl, her deer-like gaze troubled, wilts helpless; the friend, holding two great fears like the worthy who stand between two great kings driven to war, cannot bear it either, and asks the mother to hear without anger how the protecting deed the two of them dared alone, without weighing lineage, rank, looks or support, came about.
pattupattu:8:23-34.nuance: The simile of the go-between standing between two kings bent on war brings puram diplomacy into akam: the friend's two fears are that the father will be shamed and that the girl will die, and like an envoy she can serve one side only by speaking to the other. Lines 30 to 32 admit the act was undertaken without the weighing of family and fortune that a marriage arranged by kin would have made.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl's resolve to keep the secret union even beyond this life: kalavu

comparisons.vehicle: கன்மீக் கடவு மிருபெரு வேந்தர் வினையிடை நின்ற சான்றோர் போல
comparisons.tenor: the friend caught between fear of the family and fear for the girl

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the text addresses அன்னாய் (line 1); whether the foster mother or the mother is meant is not said

pattupattu:8:35-53.reading: The friend recounts the day: the mother sent them to drive birds from the small millet, whose great ripe heads bent like the drooping trunk of a pearl-tusked elephant that has fed on bamboo, and to come home at sunset; they climbed the tiger-safe platform the hill watchman had built in a tree, took up in turn the cane sling, clapper and rattle, and in the heat of the day, as birds made for their roosts, clouds drew up the sea, mingled with the wind, thundered like a drum and poured on the hill with lightning like the bright spear Murugan raises against his foes.
pattupattu:8:35-53.nuance: The mother herself sent the girls to the field (நீ விடுத்தலின், line 39), so the friend's story makes the mother's own errand the occasion of the meeting. Murugan enters only as the vehicle of a simile for lightning, the same god the mother's rites in lines 5 and 6 had been addressing.
pattupattu:8:35-53.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 35-50 and 51-66: the sentence of the storm runs on past line 50 and closes at பொழிந்தென in line 53; line 54 turns to the waterfall where the girls bathe.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field, the parrot-scaring and the watch platform are kurinji's native things

comparisons.tenor: the bent heads of ripe millet

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the text addresses அன்னாய் (line 1); whether the foster mother or the mother is meant is not said

pattupattu:8:54-61.reading: From the great peak the clear water came down in a white waterfall like shining cloth; with desire that would not stop they bathed in it, plunged into the spreading pool like poured crystal, sang on the echoing slope, wrung and dried their dark braided hair hanging down their backs, and their eyes reddened inside from the water.
pattupattu:8:54-61.nuance: The reddened eyes (உள்ளகம் சிவந்த கண்ணேம்) are the effect of long play in the water, the first sign in the story of the girls' freedom on the hill before the man appears.
pattupattu:8:54-61.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 51-66: the bathing begins at line 54 and closes with கண்ணேம் in line 61; the catalogue of flowers starts at the end of line 61, where வள்ளிதழ் qualifies the காந்தள் of line 62, so the next unit begins at line 62.

thinai_evidence.note: waterfall, mountain pool and echoing slope

pattupattu:8:62-82.reading: The friend begins the list of the flowers they gathered: bright red kaanthal with large petals, aambal, anichcham, kuvalai of the cool pond, kurinji, vetchi, red-stemmed veri, sweet mango, manichchigai, unthoozh, koovilam, fire-like erutham, sulli, kooviram, vadavanam, vaagai, kudasam, eruvai, seruvilai, karuvilai, payini, vaani, kuravam, pasumpidi, vakulam, kaayaa, aavirai, veral, sooral, poolai, kurunarungkanni, marutham, kongam, pongam, thilakam, paathiri, serunthi, athiral, sanbagam, karanthai, kulavi, mango, thillai, paalai, mullai, kullai, pidavam, sirumaaradam, vaazhai, valli, neythal, thaazhai, thalavam, thaamarai, gnaazhal, mauval, kogudi, sedal, semmal and kurali.
pattupattu:8:62-82.nuance: The list (it runs to line 96) is the girls' play turned into an inventory of every landscape's flowers, sea-shore thaazhai and gnaazhal and field lotus and marutham beside hill kaanthal: the flowers say nothing about the lovers, but they show the girls free and at play just before the man comes. Many of the names cannot now be matched to a plant with certainty; the senses given are only for the common ones.
pattupattu:8:62-82.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 51-66 and 67-82: the list of flowers that the girls gathered starts in line 62 (after the bathing, which closes in line 61) and is divided at line 82, where the core unit also ends.

thinai_evidence.note: the girls gather on the hill; kurinji and kaanthal lead the list, with flowers of every land among them

pattupattu:8:83-98.reading: The list goes on: kodal, kaithai, honey-rich vazhai, kaanji, neythal with clustered buds smelling of toddy, paangar, maraam, thanakkam, eengai, ilavam, hanging konrai, adumbu, aathi, long-stemmed avarai, pakanrai, palaasam, pindi, vanji, piththigam, sinthuvaaram, thumbai, thuzhaay, bright thonri, nanthi, naravam, punnaagam, paaram, peeram, kurukkaththi, aaram, kaazhvai, punnai, narantham, naagam, the flower that smells at midnight, kurunthu, vengai and others, with large puzhagu red as spread lac; roaming the rich forest they gathered them all and heaped them on the wide rock the rain had washed.
pattupattu:8:83-98.nuance: The heap of flowers on the rain-washed rock (வான்கண் கழீஇய அகலறைக் குவைஇ) ends the list and gives it a place: the flowers of every land are gathered onto one hill rock, as the whole idyll gathers its world into one day's story. Several names in this half of the list (பாரம், பீரம், நந்தி, காழ்வை) cannot be identified with confidence.

thinai_evidence.note: the heap is made on the wide hill rock, and vengai closes the list

pattupattu:8:99-106.reading: On the slope of the cross-lying hill, where the birds' noise sounds like instruments, the girls now and then sent out clear strong-breathed calls to drive off the parrots, tied leaf skirts of plucked petals and leaves about their waists, bound garlands of many kinds on their soft dark hair, and sat in the cool shade of the asoka, whose tender shoots shine like fire and drop pollen.
pattupattu:8:99-106.nuance: The leaf skirt (தழை) is the dress the hero of kurinji often brings as a love gift; here the girls make their own, so they are still unclaimed when he arrives in the next lines.
pattupattu:8:99-106.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 99-113: the girls' play closes with இருந்தனமாக in line 106; line 107 begins the long description of the man who came.

thinai_evidence.note: parrot-scaring and the asoka of the hill slope

pattupattu:8:107-127.reading: Then a man appeared: his dark sapphire-coloured hair washed with butter-smoothed fragrant tagaram, dried with the fingers, scented with agil smoke, and loud with striped bees humming like a lute; on his head, to inspire awe, a cool garland of chosen flowers of every colour from hill, field, branch and pool, with a chaplet of white palm strips; a pitthigam garland curved behind, red asoka shoots tucked in and tender leaves swaying on his strong shoulders; sandal on his broad chest, an old fragrant garland shining with his ornaments; a painted banded bow in his large hand, arrows chosen, a finely worked belt tied tight, and bright warrior's anklets rubbing his fine feet as he walked.
pattupattu:8:107-127.nuance: Line 113 has his garland gathered from hill, field, branch and pool, the same reach across lands as the girls' list of flowers: he comes dressed in what they had just gathered. The warrior's anklet (கழல்) and the painted bow make him a hunter-chief rather than a plain hunter.
pattupattu:8:107-127.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 99-113 and 114-129: the description of the man's dress and weapons runs from line 107 and closes at கலாவ in line 127; lines 128 and 129 belong with the hounds of line 131, which they describe.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill hunter with bow and arrows, wearing flowers of the hill

pattupattu:8:128-145.reading: His hounds, with teeth like sharp sprouts and strong claws, fierce like his many-speared young warriors who have seen the backs of enemies and laid waste the frontier, angry at every approach, came round the girls with unblinking eyes; the girls rose trembling, their feet faltering, bewildered and distressed; he came, handsome as a bull among cows that has fought off and driven away a rival, and fearing they would take fright, spoke soft sweet words, praised their hair and their looks and said that he had lost a beast that came this way; when they gave no answer he was troubled and asked whether even speaking with him was a blame, if they would not tell him of the beast.
pattupattu:8:128-145.nuance: The question about a lost beast (கெடுதி) is a pretext and the girls' silence is a rule of modesty, not rudeness: the man's reply, that speaking with him is no blame, names exactly the fear of blame that keeps them silent. Lines 128 and 129 can also be taken as describing his companions, who come with him; the reading here takes இளைஞரின் as the comparison for the hounds.
pattupattu:8:128-145.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 114-129 and 130-145: lines 128 and 129 (the young warriors) are the vehicle of a simile for the hounds of line 131, so the unit begins at 128; it ends at the core boundary, line 145, where the man's question closes.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunter's hounds and the hunter asking after his lost game

comparisons.vehicle: மாறுபொரு தோட்டிய புகல்வின் வேறுபுலத் தாகாண் விடையி
comparisons.tenor: the man coming, proud and handsome

pattupattu:8:146-165.reading: He broke a flowering branch where bees settled humming like the strings a master of the paalai mode plucks, swung it proudly as one swings at an elephant that defies the goad, silenced the loud cries of his band and stood waiting for their word; just then, in a short-posted hut thatched with millet stalks, the field watchman, served honey-pressed toddy by his doe-eyed wife, drank and grew merry, and when the watch slackened an elephant broke into the great field; the watchman, unable to bear the loss, strung his snake-like bow, the whistling men shot arrows and raised a din that rang through the forest, and the maddened elephant, trumpeting like thunder of the rains, striking the ground with its trunk, in fierce musth and breaking trees, came at the girls like Death.
pattupattu:8:146-165.nuance: The watchman's drinking is what lets the elephant in, so the poem makes a small domestic lapse the cause of the meeting that the friend calls களிறுதரு புணர்ச்சி in line 212. மடங்கல் in line 165 may be the lion or Death; either way it is the vehicle of the simile. Lines 151 and 152 can also be read as the girls silencing their own loud companions; the reading here gives the act to the man.
pattupattu:8:146-165.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 146-169: the elephant's charge closes with எதிர்தர in line 165; line 166 begins the girls' flight to the man.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet watchman's hut and the wild elephant raiding the field

comparisons.tenor: the man swinging the flowered branch

pattupattu:8:166-186.reading: Not knowing where to escape, the girls, bangles jangling, forgetting shame, ran and clung to him trembling like peacocks seized by a spirit; he drew a long feathered arrow and drove it with great force into the noble elephant's face, so that blood gushed down over it and its spotted brow was torn, and it gave way and turned its back; the girls, still holding hands as tightly as the circle of women possessed by Murugan dancing round the thick trunk of the kadamba, trembled like a plantain on a bank beaten by a foaming flood; the noble man told the girl not to fear, that he would enjoy her beauty, stroked her bright brow, thought long, looked at the friend's face and smiled, and though shame and awe made her pull away at once, he would not let her go but drew her close and embraced her.
pattupattu:8:166-186.nuance: Kapilar sets the love union inside the moment of terror: the girls' clinging to the man for safety becomes the embrace. That he looks at the friend's face and smiles (என்முகம் நோக்கி நக்கனன், line 183) makes the friend a witness, which is why she can now speak to the mother. The comparison to Murugan's possessed women, seized by the god, echoes the rites of lines 5 and 6, where the mother thinks a god has seized the girl.
pattupattu:8:166-186.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 146-169, 170-185 and 186-201: the flight and rescue begin at உய்விடம் in line 166 and the sentence closes with the embrace, முயங்கலின், in line 186; அவ்வழி in the same line opens the description of the man's hill.

thinai_evidence.note: the first union of the lovers: punarthal

comparisons.tenor: the girls trembling as they cling to him
the girls holding hands in a ring
the girls' clasped hands that do not part

pattupattu:8:187-199.reading: There, in the long rock pool into which ripe pepper had fallen and sweet mangoes dropped, mixed with honey the birds had scattered, the fragrant jackfruit that burst and fell had ripened into toddy, and a peacock drank it thinking it water and staggered like a rope-dancer at a big town's festival keeping time to a well-matched band, drooping like the goddesses of the hill: such is the slope of the lord of the hill country, whose peaks touching the sky are spread with kaanthal flowers like a field spread with new cloth.
pattupattu:8:187-199.nuance: A peacock drunk on toddy that fruit has made by itself in a rock pool is Kapilar's image of the hill's unasked plenty (Akananuru 2 uses the same rock pool and the same toddy for a monkey). Read as iraicchi it would point to the girl who took joy unplanned, but the peacock does nothing a person of the situation does, so it is scene; the description praises the land of the man the girl has chosen.
pattupattu:8:187-199.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 186-201: the description of the man's hill begins after முயங்கலின் in line 186 (அவ்வழி) and closes with its subject குன்றுகெழு நாடன் in line 199; his words begin in line 200.

thinai_evidence.note: the rock pool, kaanthal, jackfruit and peacock of the hill

pattupattu:8:200-214.reading: Understanding the girl's heart, the man of great strength whom they desired assured her, making virtue the raft: 'In a rich house that does not stint those who come, with pots of rice as for a festival and doors opened wide, where many eat rice rich with ghee and fresh fat, it will be fitting for me to eat with you, noble one, what is left after we feed guests with our blameless kin'; then, praising the god on the high peak with joined hands, he swore a binding oath in truth and drank the sweet clear water, and their hearts were at rest; so they spent that day of the union the elephant brought, in the hard cleft, in a flowered grove that even the dwellers of heaven would desire.
pattupattu:8:200-214.nuance: The oath is sworn to the hill god and sealed by drinking water, and its content is a household: he promises a house of open doors and guests, not a feeling. The word for the oath, வஞ்சினம், is the one puram uses for a warrior's vow before battle. களிறுதரு புணர்ச்சி (line 212) names the convention, the union an elephant brings about.
pattupattu:8:200-214.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 186-201, 202-213 and 214-233: the man's words begin with உள்ளினன் கொண்டு in line 200, and the day of union closes with அப்பகல் கழிப்பி in line 214; line 215 turns to sunset.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover's oath after the union: kurinji's punarthal and its pledge

comparisons.tenor: the pots of rice in his house
his assurance, on which she could cross her fear

pattupattu:8:215-233.reading: As the day went, the many-rayed sun bowed and hid behind the hill; deer crowded at the foot of trees, cows calling their calves filled the common, the curve-beaked anril cried with a horn's moan in the fronds of the tall palmyra, snakes spat out their gems, cowherds in many places played clear notes on ambal flutes, water lilies opened, women in rich houses lit lamps, brahmins did the evening rite, forest men lit torches on their sky-high watch platforms, the sky darkened round the great hill, the forest roared and flocks of birds cried; seeing the evening hasten on like the battle of an angry king, the man took the girl's forearm and said, 'When your people give her, we will hold a good wedding the whole land will know; for these few days, bright-jewelled ones, do not be troubled.'
pattupattu:8:215-233.nuance: The sunset is drawn with mullai's hour and things, cows to their calves and the cowherd's flute, alongside kurinji's forest men and their torches; the evening is the hour when the lovers must part, and the man answers it with a promise of public marriage (நாடறி நன்மணம்), the first word of வரைவு in the poem. The simile of a king's army advancing is the second puram image the friend uses, after the two kings of line 27.
pattupattu:8:215-233.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 214-233: line 214 (அப்பகல் கழிப்பி) closes the day of union and goes with the previous unit; the sunset begins with எல்லை செல்ல in line 215 and the unit still ends at the man's promise in line 233.

thinai_evidence.note: forest men's watch platforms round the great hill; the evening's mullai things are borrowed

pattupattu:8:234-246.reading: Having spoken kind good words in full, he came with them like a bull with its mate, brought them to the drinking ford at the gate of the old town where the drums never sleep, and left; since then, with the same desire as that day, he has made night-coming his habit, and every time he comes, if the guards hurry about, if the fierce dog barks, if you wake, if the moon comes out, never getting sweet sleep on her soft bamboo-like shoulders, he goes back without ever being angry; he has not strayed in youth, nor left his station through wealth; and the girl, thinking of the nature of his secret coming in that dreaded town, consoles herself.
pattupattu:8:234-246.nuance: The friend gives the mother a character witness: the man keeps coming, is turned back by every hindrance and is never angry, and has not lapsed through youth or wealth (lines 243 to 245). The list of hindrances is told to the girl's mother, who is herself one of them (நீ துயில் எழினும).
pattupattu:8:234-246.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 234-249: the account of the man's nightly visits closes with தேற்றி in line 246; line 247 turns to the girl's tears, which the next unit carries to the end of the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the night tryst and its hindrances: kurinji's punarthal at midnight

comparisons.tenor: the man coming home with the girls

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the text addresses அன்னாய் (line 1); whether the foster mother or the mother is meant is not said

pattupattu:8:247-261.reading: Her large bold cloud-dark eyes, drooping like flowers beaten by water, weep and their tears drip on her breast; every day her beauty wastes like a peacock caught in a net, and she weeps whenever she thinks that at night his clustered hill's clefts hold inescapable sorrows: the cave-dwelling tiger, the yali and the bear, the hollow-horned wild cattle and the elephant, the cruel fierce thunder and the spirits, the prey-seeking snake, the crooked-legged crocodile, idangar and karaam that move in the deep whirlpools, the slippery places, the narrow broken paths, the ghouls, the pythons and the rest.
pattupattu:8:247-261.nuance: The poem ends not on the union but on the danger of the night path, which is the friend's strongest argument: the mother cannot keep the girl from the man, only from a marriage, and every night without one sends him through the beasts of lines 252 to 259. The netted peacock of line 250 answers the peacock of line 169: the girl who clung to him for safety is now caught.
pattupattu:8:247-261.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 234-249 and 250-261: the girl's tears begin with நீரெறி மலரின் in line 247, and the sentence they open runs to the end of the poem in line 261.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl's fear for the man who comes by night over the hill: kurinji's night tryst

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the text addresses அன்னாய் (line 1); whether the foster mother or the mother is meant is not said

links.note: In Akananuru 98 the girl fears that the mother's velan rite, held for a sickness read as Murugan's seizure, will expose the secret; in the idyll the mother's diviners and offerings to many gods have already failed, and the friend makes that failure the ground for telling her.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show that the misread sickness and its useless rite are the hinge of the kurinji plot: the short poem stops at the girl's dread of exposure, and Kapilar's idyll starts from the same point and turns the failed cure into the friend's reason to disclose the love and press for marriage.

links.note: The Kural likens those fallen from their station to hair fallen from the head; the friend says broken jewels can be rejoined but lost worth and fame cannot be washed clean even by sages.
links.teaches: The friend uses the Kural's idea that a fall in standing is beyond repair as an argument for speaking at once, not for keeping quiet: because a girl's good name cannot be restored once it is lost, the secret has to come out before gossip costs her it, so the maxim on honour drives the plot of disclosure.

links.note: Kovur Kizhar stands between two Chola kings at war and tells them that whichever loses, their own house loses; the friend says she holds two great fears like the worthy who stand between two great kings bent on war.
links.teaches: Purananuru 45 shows from inside the position the idyll's simile names, the mediator who can win nothing for either side: so the friend's double fear, for the father's honour and for the girl's life, is modelled on the puram envoy's predicament, and the akam go-between borrows the role of the poet who speaks between kings.

links.note: Both are told by the friend to the mother in disclosure: in Akananuru 48 a garlanded hunter with a bow asks the girls which way the beast went; in the idyll the hunter says he has lost a beast that came this way and, when they keep silent, asks whether even speaking with him is a blame.
links.teaches: Read together, the hunter's question about a lost beast stands out as the conventional opening of the hill meeting reported in அறத்தொடு நிற்றல், and the idyll supplies what the short poem leaves to the mother's wit: the girls' silence out of fear of blame and the man's answer to that fear.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai places Murugan at the veri ground and under the fresh-flowered kadamba; the idyll compares the terrified girls holding hands to the ring of women possessed by Neduvel dancing round a kadamba trunk.
links.teaches: The possession dance that Thirumurugatruppadai describes as worship is used by Kapilar as the image for the girls at the very moment the love begins, so the god-seizure the mother wrongly suspects in the opening lines comes back as a simile for what really happened.

links.note: Both poems by Kapilar have toddy made by ripe jackfruit in a long rock pool (பாறை நெடுஞ்சுனை, விளைந்த தேறல்) drunk unknowingly by a creature: a monkey that cannot climb and sleeps, a peacock that staggers like a rope-dancer.
links.teaches: The same poet uses one formula for two jobs: in Akananuru 2 the drunk monkey is an argument that the lover can easily find the joy he plans, while in the idyll the drunk peacock only praises the plenty of the lover's land, which shows that in Kapilar the image's force depends on where it stands in the speech, not on the image itself.

links.note: The Kural says household life and its guarding of goods exist to care for guests; the man's oath promises a house of open doors where he and the girl will eat what is left after feeding guests.
links.teaches: The Kural's rule that the household exists for guests is already in the idyll the language in which a hill man pledges marriage: what he swears to give the girl is not a feeling but a guest-feeding house, so the ethic of virundhu was the content of the promise before it was a maxim.

links.note: Akananuru 122 lists the hindrances that keep the lover away (the sleepless town, the mother, guards who hurry, the dog, the moon); the idyll lists nearly the same (guards hurrying, the fierce dog, the mother waking, the moon) as what turns him back every night.
links.teaches: In Akananuru 122 the girl uses the catalogue of hindrances to complain about their secret love, whereas the friend in the idyll gives it to the mother as proof of the man's constancy, since he goes back each time without anger, so the same list can work as a lament or as a testimonial depending on who is listening.

links.note: In Akananuru 112 the friend tells the man who has come at night of the bear and the tiger on his path and asks why he does not marry; the idyll ends with the girl weeping over the tiger, bear, elephant, crocodiles and spirits of his night path, told to the mother.
links.teaches: The dangers of the night path press for marriage from both sides: in Akananuru 112 they are told to the man to make him propose, and in the idyll to the mother to make the family consent, so the same catalogue is used as leverage on whichever party is holding back.

new_concepts.gloss: disclosure of a secret love to the family, usually by the friend to the mother or foster mother, so that the lovers may be married; literally, standing by what is right
new_concepts.label_source: text: the colophon thurai of Kurinjippattu

source_issues: Line 42 வலத்த: tamilvu reads வலந்த (woven), which fits the cane implements better; our text is kept.
Line 87 யடும்பம ராத்தி is a genuine அடும்பு + அமர் + ஆத்தி, not a lost comitative ending; karu forms are copied as printed.
Line 142 னென்றென: tamilvu reads என்றனன், which the sense needs (he said); our text is kept.
Line 89 prints சிந் துவாரம் with a space inside the one word சிந்துவாரம்.
The text is printed in the old joined style, so a word whose last consonant fuses with the next vowel is given in karu as printed (for example காந்த ளாம்ப in line 62 gives the forms காந்த and ளாம்ப).
